III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00629

The holy Imams repeatedly taught that the secret entrusted to humanity was their walayat: the special relationship with God that makes them the “friends of God” (awliya Allah) and the guardians of God's cause (al-amr al-ilahi). Their mission runs alongside and completes the mission of the prophets (nobowwat). They guide those who choose them as their friends and teachers towards the hidden, spiritual meaning of the revelations given to the prophets.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00630

To take the Imams as friends is to love them. The sources call this devotion walayat or mahabbat, often using the two words interchangeably. In loving them, their followers direct their love towards the divine Face made visible through them.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00631
We can now see why, in Shiism, Islam as a prophetic religion is also a religion of love. Those who take the Imams as friends are saved from perishing, because the divine Face does not perish.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00632

This love is also why the believer's testimony to walayat is the necessary completion of a threefold declaration of faith (shahadat). First comes the testimony to the One: God beyond all being, beyond words and beyond anything we can say about Him.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00633

Second comes the testimony to the prophetic mission through which God reveals His Names, qualities, and acts to humanity. Third comes the testimony to the Imams and their walayat. The believer's loving devotion to them is part of faith (iman) itself, because it recognises the Imam as the guide who reveals the hidden meaning of those divine Names, qualities, and acts.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00634

This is why Shiite teachers agree that these three testimonies belong together. The declaration of God's oneness (tawhid) relates to the declaration of the prophetic mission in the same way that the prophetic mission relates to the declaration of the Twelve Imams. Or, looking from the other direction, walayat stands in relation to prophecy just as prophecy stands in relation to God's oneness.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00635

None of the three can be separated from the others. The believer's testimony to the Twelve Imams is the response, deep within the heart, to God's own love for them. It completes and seals the whole declaration. Without walayat—without the loving devotion carried by that word—faith is not merely empty; it is not faith (iman) in the fullest sense at all.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00636

This threefold testimony has, in a mysterious sense, been written into every universe, at every level where God becomes manifest. For it concerns the first Principle and two movements that begin and end in that Principle: the movement by which creation comes forth, and the movement by which everything returns to its source. These are mabda' and ma'ad, origin and return.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00637

The same pairing appears throughout religious life. There is tanzil, the descent of revelation, and ta'wil, the spiritual interpretation that leads the revealed words back to their original, higher meaning. There is shariat, religious law, and haqiqat, the spiritual truth at its heart.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00638

There is nobowwat, the mission of the prophets, and the Imamate, the mission of the Imams. At each level where the divine becomes manifest, the beings belonging to that world were asked to make the same threefold commitment (mithaq). This continued all the way down to the world of human beings on earth.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00639

Shiite scholars also agree on the meaning of the scene of the first Covenant, described in Qur'an 7:171, where God asks humanity, in a realm beyond ordinary history, “Am I not your Lord?” (Alastu bi-rabbikum?). At the same moment that Adam's descendants were asked to recognise God's oneness, they were also asked to accept the messages of the prophets still to come and the spiritual guidance of their Imams.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00640

Humanity answered “yes,” but the scholars acknowledge that not everyone gave that answer in the same way. As we have already seen, Adam's humanity held within it the pure light of all the prophetic messages to come. It is this light within Adam that answers “yes”; it is the part of him that speaks. The story of sacred history makes the point when the Prophet tells the Imam, “You and I were the first to answer yes.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00641

Humanity accepted the terrifying burden before which the heavens, the earth, and the mountains had trembled (Qur'an 33:72). And what did humanity accept? The very secret of God's appearances: the mystery of how the Unknowable reveals His Face while remaining hidden within the figures through which He is revealed. This is what makes the bond between the Imams and the hidden meaning of revelation permanent.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00642

Here, too, a remarkable way of reading scripture opens up. In Shiite spirituality, it develops something comparable to the Renaissance Platonists' theme of the dignity of the human being (De dignitate hominis). To accept the burden of such an overwhelming secret, the human being had to be both reckless and unaware.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00643

Yet in this setting, both words become terms of praise. Haydar Amoli speaks of magnificent secrets here, of matters whose depths cannot be measured. He devoted an entire treatise to them, The Treatise on the Trust (Risalat al-amana), though unfortunately we have not yet managed to find a manuscript.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00644
We can, however, recover something of its argument from the Shiite commentaries inspired by the same Qur'anic verse (33:72).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00645

What, then, are this recklessness and ignorance shown by the human being in accepting God's trust? The recklessness is an act of courage directed against oneself. Adam, standing for humanity, accepts the divine secret by setting aside his own separate self before God's absolute Self. He chooses to know nothing that is other than God—not even to acknowledge that anything other than God exists.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00646

At this point, the mystery of humanity meets the mystery of God. The secret of declaring God's oneness is to deny independent reality to everything that is not God, and to know that only God truly is. Haydar Amoli calls this oneness at the level of being, or ontological tawhid. Theological tawhid—the belief that God is one—is only its first stage. If we stop there, we risk falling into what he sees as a kind of idolatry in our very idea of God.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00647

When something goes beyond its proper limit, it can turn into its opposite. That is what happened with Adam's recklessness and ignorance. At first they were a heroic daring, a magnificent unawareness, without which he could never have carried God's secrets. In that sense, they truly were qualities to admire. By gathering all his spiritual strength—his Minuta—Adam lifted a burden greater than his strength should have allowed.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00648

Someone asked him—who it was, the symbolic story does not say—“You thought yourself stronger than you were. Didn't you know how crushing the burden would be?” Adam replied, “I knew nothing apart from God.” That was how he could bear the hidden truth, the secret of those to whom God had said, “You are My Face.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00649

Qazi Sa'id Qummi describes this state of knowledge through an arresting image. In a spiritual circle, unlike a physical one, “the centre surrounds the circumference.” The mind, as the centre, embraces all the lights that make up its knowledge.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00650

Hence the saying: “Knowledge is a single point; it is the ignorant who turn it into many.” That multiplicity appears when we begin to recognise something other than God. For Qazi Sa'id Qummi, this is the ignorance hinted at by Qur'an 33:72.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00651

As long as Adam remains unaware that anything other than God can truly exist, his magnificent unawareness gives him the strength to carry the weight of the divine secrets. He is a bearer of God, a theophore.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00652

But the moment God is no longer enough for him, he begins to recognise something outside God—and by recognising it, he sets it apart as something other. The figures through which God appears are not God Himself. So why, Adam begins to ask, should he need them to reach God? And if he no longer needs them, why should he not reach the hidden truth directly, without the outward form that makes it visible and known?
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00653

Once he has set up this world of “otherness,” he too is something other than God. Why, then, should he need anyone else? His once-magnificent unawareness turns into a dizzying pride in himself. He becomes blind to the claims of others and wants to take for himself everything that belongs to them. This is the fall that sacred history tells through symbols.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00654
The divine secret spoken of in Qur'an 33:72 was the walayat of the Imams.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00655

We can now understand why it was represented by the tree in Paradise that Adam was forbidden to touch or dishonour. In his interpretation of this verse, Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq says that Adam was shown the divine, more-than-human nature of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones, shining in the blazing glory of the Throne. Adam wondered: could there really be a humanity greater than his own, created “in heaven” before him?
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00656

Yet their light—the light of that heavenly humanity—was precisely the trust he had accepted and promised to protect. When they appeared in the human world, these beings were to come from his own descendants.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00657

But Adam was no longer content with that role. He wanted to possess for himself what had been entrusted to him. Overcome by ambition, he tried to go beyond his proper place and claim immediately the rank that would only be made visible at the end of his line, through the one called the “Seal of walayat.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00658

That was what it meant to touch the forbidden tree and break the rule that sacred secrets must be disclosed only to those ready to receive them. The tree symbolises both the walayat of the Imams, whom Adam wanted to replace, and their knowledge: the knowledge of that humanity made of light (bashar nuriyun). Adam wanted to reach it before his time, though he lacked both the strength and the capacity to bear it. In the words of Qur'an 33:72, he was “reckless and ignorant.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00659

Qazi Sa'id Qummi explains the problem with unusual depth. The person who knows and the things that person knows must exist at corresponding levels. What we know becomes actual within us, much as food becomes part of the person who eats it. By touching the forbidden tree of Knowledge and “eating” its fruit—the things it offered him to know—Adam forced that knowledge down to his own level. And in doing so, he himself “descended from Paradise.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00660

What makes this interpretation so striking is the connection it draws between Adam's disobedience and the violation of hidden spiritual knowledge. Shiite spiritual knowledge is the inner meaning of prophetic revelation. It had been rejected and persecuted by those whom the tradition calls “the reckless and the ignorant,” so its teachers could hardly fail to see the importance of this story. Adam's transgression is really a movement backwards: a fall to a lower kind of knowing, where the ability to understand symbols is lost.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00661

There is no longer any sacred knowledge connecting the human mind with worlds beyond this one, and no awareness of spiritual realities beyond the senses. By casting off the divine secrets he had accepted, and betraying the trust placed in him, humanity becomes agnostic about these spiritual realities. In this sense, Qur'an 33:72 binds together the mystery of God and the mystery of humanity.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00662

Just as striking is the agreement between Ismaili and Twelver Shiite interpretations of Adam's fault. Both see it not as a drama of the flesh, but as a drama of human knowledge. In Ismaili sacred history, Adam was appointed prophet and Imam at the start of our present “cycle of concealment” (dawr al-satr). Conditions in this cycle are entirely different from those of the earlier “cycle of disclosure” (dawr al-kashf). Even the rules of knowledge have changed. Human beings can now perceive spiritual things only by understanding the links and correspondences between visible things and invisible realities.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00663

But knowledge through such correspondences—the ability to recognise symbols—depends on the partnership of two sides: shariat and haqiqat, the outward religious law and its inner truth; the written words and the spiritual knowledge they express; the visible form and the hidden meaning.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00664

At Iblis's suggestion, Adam tried to gain a kind of knowledge beyond his reach. He wanted to grasp the hidden spiritual reality directly, stripping away the outward form through which that reality shines and makes itself known. Some fashionable theologians today speak of “demystifying” and “demythologising,” without fully realising what they are doing.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00665

Adam was trying to seize, by force, a knowledge that belongs essentially to the Resurrection, and that only the final Imam of the cycle, the Qa'im, is appointed to reveal. Because that knowledge exceeded his capacity, it slipped away from him. All he found was his own nakedness: the darkness within him, his own ignorance. He tried to strip the hidden meaning bare, but what he exposed was his inability to know it.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00666

To lose the language of symbols is to lose the garment of God's Word, which had surrounded him like a robe of light and driven out his inner darkness. What could remain? Only the memory of the symbols he had lost. And that is what it means, in the story, for the human being to cover his nakedness with “leaves from the garden.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00667

We can therefore understand what Shiite spiritual interpretation, and Haydar Amoli in particular, hear in the Qur'anic commands to remain faithful to a trust. They hear a command on which their own spiritual tradition depends: “Believers, do not betray God and His Messenger by betraying the trusts placed in your care, when you know what you are doing” (8:27). We have seen what this trust is.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00668
We can now understand that it can be betrayed in two different ways, both leading to the same result.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00669

The first is to try to take it by force: to strip away the outward covering through which the hidden meaning becomes visible, and to abandon the duty of guarding sacred secrets. That hands the secret over to people who are not ready for it.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00670

Unable to understand it, they can only distort it and do violence to its meaning. They confuse spiritual resurrection with social revolt, for example. Their efforts no longer even approach the point at which the idea of being born anew—a spiritual birth (wiladat ruhaniya)—can begin to make sense.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00671

The second way is simply to deny that the trust exists. And the first betrayal makes this denial much easier: once the hidden meaning has been stripped of its true character and distorted, it becomes all the easier to reject. Such outright rejection takes many forms, from the devout refusal of the scholars of religious law and their social successors to acknowledge spiritual knowledge, to the narrow view of the world held by technical experts who recognise only what can be measured and used. The first group reduces knowledge of spiritual realities to the level of natural or social facts.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00672
The second refuses to recognise spiritual knowledge at all. It is easy for them to agree.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00673

When the hidden meaning is rejected, the outward meaning (zahir) also suffers a radical loss. Religious law (shariat) cannot remain true to itself without spiritual understanding (irfan and haqiqat). It makes no sense to speak of an “orthodox” Sufism if that means Sufism without inner knowledge. Left entirely on its own, the visible world no longer points beyond itself to the invisible. It becomes a still life, a dried-out husk, an empty chrysalis.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00674

Religion reduced to law and social rules, and nature reduced to what technical science can investigate and exploit, are two faces of the same decline. Turning spiritual life into something purely secular and social goes hand in hand with the drive for power of a useful but spiritually blind science. This is why Western technology can threaten traditional Shiite Islam only to the extent that Shiite Islam has already abandoned or betrayed the divine trust entrusted to humanity.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00675

That trust weighs even more heavily on Adam now that he carries it with longing and repentance, having recovered it only after a long search. One of Imam Ja'far's conversations includes a beautiful symbolic story. It strongly recalls the famous Hymn of the Pearl in the Gnostic Acts of Thomas, and may help us understand the pearl as a symbol, and the search for the pearl as a spiritual journey.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00676
We will encounter another echo of the same theme in Suhrawardi's Tale of the Western Exile (Book II).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00677

The Imam asks one of his disciples, “Do you know what the Black Stone is?”—the stone set into a corner of the Kaaba in Mecca. He explains that the Black Stone had once been an angel, given to Adam as a companion in Paradise to remind him of his promise, his covenant (mithaq).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00678

More precisely, this was the angel who carried the entrusted secret at the very centre of Adam's being. For the events described by the Qur'anic verses of the Covenant (7:171) and the Trust (33:72) take place in the malakut: the angelic world of the soul, which is itself the hidden, spiritual side of the world we see.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00679

When God turned towards Adam again in response to his repentance, He changed the angel into a white pearl and sent it out of Paradise towards Adam as he travelled down the road of exile. Adam did not recognise it at first. To him, it looked like an ordinary stone. Through repentance, he had to peel away the covering that hid the pearl. Then it took its original form, spoke to him, reminded him of his promise, and awakened the memory of his homeland of light. Adam wept.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00680

Once again, the angel was hidden, this time in the form of a precious stone. Adam carried it on his shoulder all the way from Ceylon to Mecca. Whenever he grew tired, the angel Gabriel, who travelled beside him, took the weight and carried it for a while. That is how Adam's angel—the hidden, spiritual meaning at the heart of Adam—came into this world. The Black Stone was placed in one corner of the Temple at the centre of the world, just as the angel was at the centre of Adam's being.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00681

The entrusted secret, the angel hidden within Adam, is the weight of the divine mysteries that Adam carries after rediscovering the pearl of spiritual knowledge. So great is that weight that Gabriel, the angel of Knowledge and Revelation, must help him bear it.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00682

This is why the Shiite Imams repeatedly gave the teaching we have already encountered: “Our cause is difficult, and its burden is heavy. No one can bear it except an angel of the highest rank, a prophet sent by God, or a believer whose heart God has tested for faith.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00683

As we will see in Chapter V, this saying introduces their whole teaching about hidden spiritual truth. The believers who have passed the test are those Shiites who answered the first Covenant with an unreserved “yes,” those who, in the words of the tradition, “were created from a ray of the light of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00684

Imam Ja'far speaks of them again in the long hadith we quoted earlier (p. 52): “Our cause is difficult,” he says. “To uphold it, we need minds in which dawn is breaking, hearts burning with light, healthy souls, and beautiful natures. God has already received the pledge of our Shiite followers [...]. O God, let them live our life and die our death. Do not let the enemy overcome them. For if You let the enemy overcome them, there will be no one left in this world to worship You.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00685

These are the witnesses who carry Shiism in its fullest sense and keep the chain of spiritual knowledge alive in this world (silsilat al-irfan). They can bear the entrusted secret and take up the cause of the Imams because they are the believers “whose hearts God has tested for faith.” This is why there were never more than a handful of true followers around the Imams. It is to people like these that we hear the First Imam refer in a conversation with his disciple Komayl.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
en-book-1-ch-3-s3
3. Conversations between the First Imam and Komayl ibn Ziyad
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00686

I have in mind two conversations between the First Imam and Komayl ibn Ziyad, one of his most distinguished disciples and companions. For our purposes, the first is an introduction to the second. Few texts show more clearly what “spiritual struggle” means in the Imam's teaching, what is at stake in that struggle, and what kind of spiritual courage it requires.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00687

In the first conversation, Komayl asks, “What is gnosis—direct spiritual knowledge?” The Imam tests him with a question of his own: “What business do you have with gnosis?” He explains why it could harm them both if he poured such a secret from himself into Komayl: a vessel cannot hold more than its capacity allows, and the Imam has been commanded to put each thing in its proper place.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00688

Komayl appeals to that very responsibility. “Can someone like you,” he asks, “disappoint a person who comes to you with a question? With your knowledge of the highest spiritual realities, and your ability to judge what each person is ready to understand, could you deny the questioner what is rightfully his? Could you leave him unable to reach his goal simply by refusing to answer? Surely not. God's command says, ‘Do not turn away the one who asks’ (Qur'an 93:10). You must answer, guided by the Prophet's instruction: ‘When you speak to people, speak to each according to their understanding.’”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00689
The Imam grants his request and begins:
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00690
Imam: “Gnosis is the unveiling of the sanctuaries of divine Majesty, though there is nothing you can point to and show.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00691
Komayl: “Tell me more.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00692
Imam: “It is the disappearance of everything uncertain, and the quiet assurance of what is known with certainty.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00693
Komayl: “Tell me more.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00694
Imam: “The veil is torn away, and the secret has prevailed.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00695
Komayl: “Tell me more.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00696

Imam: “A light rises from the dawn before time began. It shines in the temples of tawhid”—that is, within those who profess God's true oneness. (A note in the margin of one of our manuscripts adds that this light is the eternal Imam.)
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00697
Komayl: “Tell me more.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00698
Imam: “Put out the lamp. Morning has come.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00699
After that, the Imam fell silent.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00700

This conversation alone shows us that the Imams' teaching, the source of Shiite wisdom, is quite different from three familiar approaches: the reasoning through argument practised by Islamic scholastic theologians (mutakallimun), the methods of proof used by philosophers working in the Greek tradition (falasifa), and the attitude of pious ascetics who take little interest in spiritual knowledge. It is a distinctive kind of teaching, one that tends to be overlooked when Islam is discussed in the West.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00701
We have even come to mistake Shiism for a “religion of authority,” in the Western sense of that phrase, because we have largely lost our understanding of what spiritual initiation involves.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00702

Notice that the Imam does not impose a fixed formula of belief. Our authors describe the knowledge he teaches as knowledge inherited by the soul ('ilm irthi; see Chapter VI, section 4). The soul is entitled to this inheritance, and receives it, to the extent that it is capable of understanding it.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00703

The true heir is the one who can understand. No amount of clever argument can win this inheritance by force. The person's level of understanding is what gives them the right to receive it and makes them someone to whom the sacred trust can be handed over. That, precisely, was Komayl's reason for asking the Imam to answer him.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00704

The conversation is certainly difficult, and it has inspired long commentaries. Haydar Amoli, who discusses it at length in the second part of the major work we will examine later (Book IV, Chapter I), makes just one observation when he first quotes it. The key to the entire exchange, he says, lies in its final words: “After that, the Imam fell silent.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00705

For Haydar Amoli, the silence means that Komayl has been brought to the point on the spiritual path where he can see for himself. There is no longer anything to be gained by asking questions in the language of logical argument. Compared with the sun, argument is only a lamp. In the end, inner revelation and mystical experience cannot be fully expressed or shown to another person—as the Imam had hinted from the very beginning.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00706

Haydar Amoli draws two lessons from this. First, it is through silence that a person seeking spiritual knowledge reaches the goal of the search, through an experience that brings the person as close to God as is possible.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00707

Second, although the Imams revealed these divine secrets (asrar ilahiya) to their closest and most accomplished disciples, nobody is permitted to disclose them to people who are unprepared or unable to receive them. Here again we meet the solemn duty to guard the entrusted secret. Who, then, are the people who have protected and passed it on from one generation to the next?
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00708

A second conversation between the Imam and Komayl takes place in a setting of deep solitude. The Imam takes Komayl by the hand and leads him out of the city into the desert. There he lets out a deep sigh and says:
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00709
“Komayl ibn Ziyad, hearts are vessels, and the best are those with the greatest capacity. Remember what I am about to tell you.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00710

“People fall into three groups. There are the sages whose wisdom comes from God ('alim rabbani), the true masters of divine wisdom. There are those who receive their teaching and are guided towards deliverance. And there is the ordinary crowd, who follow every agitator and turn whichever way the wind blows. They are not illuminated by knowledge, and they have no solid pillar to lean on.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00711

“Komayl, knowledge is worth more than material possessions. Knowledge watches over you, whereas you must watch over your possessions. Spending wealth reduces it; sharing knowledge makes it grow. [...] Knowledge judges, while wealth is judged.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00712

“Komayl, the store of material wealth will perish. But those who possess spiritual knowledge remain alive with a life that lasts through the ages. Their bodies disappear, and others whose hearts are like theirs take their place.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00713
Then the Imam points to his own heart and continues:
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00714

“Here is knowledge in overflowing abundance! If only I could find people strong enough to carry it. Sometimes I meet someone with a quick and subtle mind, yet I cannot trust him. He uses religion to advance his worldly interests. He uses God's gifts as an excuse to rise above God's servants, and uses his learning to gain power over God's friends.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00715

“Or I meet someone who obediently follows the religious scholars but has no inner vision of his own. As soon as he meets the first difficulty, doubt enters his heart. No, neither of these men deserves my trust or can be entrusted with my spiritual knowledge. At other times, I meet someone who can never get enough pleasure and willingly lets his bodily desires lead him, or someone obsessed with gathering and hoarding wealth. Neither could ever serve as a guardian of religion. They are more like the flocks grazing in a field. Does this mean that spiritual knowledge must die whenever those who carry it die? Certainly not!
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00716

“The earth is never without people who uphold God's testimony on God's behalf, whether they do so openly or remain hidden and completely unknown. Thanks to them, God's signs and the understanding of their meaning are never lost. How many are there? Where are they? I swear by God, they are very few, but their standing is exceedingly high. Through them, God preserves the signs and proofs of the divine presence in this world until they can pass them to people like themselves and plant their seeds in kindred hearts.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00717

“For these people, spiritual knowledge reveals itself all at once, in the full truth of inner vision. They know the joy of certainty. What people weakened by an easy life find difficult, they find easy. What frightens the ignorant is familiar to them. Their bodies live in this world, but the spirits within them remain connected to the highest dwelling. Komayl! These are God's representatives on earth, calling people to the true religion. How I long to see them!”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00718

Set this solemn statement by the First Imam beside the words of Imam Ja'far quoted at the end of the previous section. Across the generations, the Imams of Shiism teach the same essential lesson. These statements, and many others like them, establish three things.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00719

First, Shiism is, at its heart, the inner meaning of Islam. Second, this inner teaching is the very teaching into which the Imams initiated their disciples, and which those disciples passed on. Third, people's different responses to this teaching—whether they receive it or reject it—divide them into three groups.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00720

The best explanation of the First Imam's statement to Komayl ibn Ziyad comes from other sayings of the Imams on the same subject. I will mention only a few, but the whole body of these teachings is of decisive importance. They show that Shiism has a calling to introduce people to a deeper teaching, to Islam's inner dimension. They therefore challenge two groups: Shiites who would rather ignore this inner meaning, and Sufis who refuse to recognise the source and foundation of their own spiritual knowledge.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00721

The witnesses described by the Imam, who uphold God's cause from generation to generation without the wider world even knowing they exist, form a spiritual community. Its order is based not on public rank or social position, but entirely on the qualities of a person's inner life. It cannot be reduced to a worldly institution or social structure.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00722

The “representatives of God on earth” are, first of all, the eleven Imams who succeed the First Imam. Beyond them are others who continue an unseen spiritual line around its mystical centre, the Hidden Imam, until the end of our present age. Without them, humanity could not continue to exist, whether it knows this or not. Here, at last, we reach the meaning of Shiism's spiritual struggle and what is at stake in it.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00723

Among the sayings that explicitly explain why Shiism has this inner dimension, one deserves particular attention. We have quoted it several times already because, with slight variations, it returns again and again. It appears in several collections, and the Imams themselves stressed its exceptional importance: “Our cause is difficult. It places a heavy demand on those who accept it. It can be borne only by an angel close to God (malak moqarrab), a prophet entrusted with a mission (nabi mursal), or a faithful believer whose heart God has tested through faith.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00724

The disciple who reports this saying from Imam Ja'far goes on: “Imam Ja'far added: Among the angels, some are close to God and others are not. Among the prophets, some are entrusted with a mission and others are not (see Chapter VI below). Among believers, some have been tested and others have not. Our cause was presented to the angels, but only those close to God accepted it. It was presented to the prophets, but only those entrusted with a mission accepted it. It was presented to believers, but only those whose hearts had been tested accepted it.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00725

The Fifth Imam, Muhammad Baqir, had already made the same point to one of his close companions: “Do you not see how difficult our cause must be, when God chose to entrust it only to angels close to Him, prophets sent on a mission, and believers whose hearts had been tested?” A commentator from the Safavid period explains the purpose of these accounts: no one can fully embrace this cause without a burning desire for it, complete acceptance of it, and a perfect love for the Imams' immaculate purity (ismat).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00726

The Sixth Imam, Ja'far, makes another statement to a close companion, repeating the word sirr—“secret”—with striking insistence. To appreciate its meaning, we need to remember that sirr does not refer only to something concealed. It can also name one of our subtle inner faculties: the innermost awareness, beyond ordinary consciousness.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00727

We will return to this saying in Chapter V, alongside the previous one, when we examine how the Qur'an's deeper meaning is understood through spiritual insight. The Imam says: “Our cause is a secret hidden within a secret (sirr mastur fi sirr), the secret of something still concealed, a secret that only another secret can teach. It is a secret upon a secret, itself hidden by a secret.”
